analysis.subject: physics
analysis.pageCoverage: Page covers historic lift equation relating Smeaton coefficient velocity wing area and lift coefficient, factors affecting lift, early coefficient values, Wright brothers experiments and wind tunnel work guiding later aircraft design.

overview.headline: Wright brothers tested historic lift equation to size wings and refine wing design

keyPoints.point: Lift was determined to depend on the square of the velocity and vary linearly with the surface area of the object
keyPoints.quote: it had been determined that lift depends on the square of the velocity and varies linearly with the surface area of the object.

keyPoints.point: Early aerodynamicists used Smeaton coefficient to represent pressure force on a flat plate moving through air
keyPoints.quote: Smeaton’s coefficient which represented the pressure force (drag) on a one foot square flat plate moving at one mile per hour through the air.

keyPoints.point: Brothers began to doubt the Smeaton value and found another value more closely approximated their data
keyPoints.quote: the brothers began to doubt the .005 value for the Smeaton coefficient

keyPoints.point: Wind tunnel testing showed the importance of wing shape and planform on the lift coefficient
keyPoints.quote: the brothers discovered the importance of wing shape on the lift coefficient

keyTerms.gloss: fraction of flat plate pressure converted to lift as described in the lift coefficient relation
keyTerms.quote: where L is the lift, k is the Smeaton coefficient, V is the velocity, A is the wing area, and cl is the lift coefficient.

keyTerms.gloss: pressure coefficient representing drag on a one foot square flat plate at one mile per hour
keyTerms.quote: k is the Smeaton coefficient, V is the velocity, A is the wing area, and cl is the lift coefficient.

keyTerms.gloss: inclination of body to flow also called angle of attack that influences lift
keyTerms.quote: the body’s inclination to the flow, also called the angle of attack.

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: Contrasting historic and modern formulations clarifies how pressure dependence and coefficient definitions evolved
componentPlan.focusQuote: The modern equation uses the dynamic pressure of the moving air for the pressure dependence, while this equation uses the Smeaton coefficient.

componentPlan.pedagogicalReason: Checking recalled values for coefficient range and design performance reinforces factual retention of historic flight data
componentPlan.focusQuote: Because of measuring inaccuracies at the time, there were many quoted values for the coefficient ranging from .0027 to .005.
